\boxed{35}

A symmetric $n \times n$ matrix $M$ of linear forms on $\mathbb{P}^3$ defines a hypersurface $X = \{\det M = 0\}$ of degree $n$. Its nodes occur precisely where $M$ drops to corank $\ge 2$ (i.e. $\operatorname{rank} \le n-2$). The locus of symmetric $n \times n$ matrices of rank $\le n-2$ has codimension $3$ in the space $\mathbb{P}^{\binom{n+1}{2}-1}$ of all symmetric matrices; intersecting it with a general linear $\mathbb{P}^3$ yields a $0$-scheme whose degree is the degree of that determinantal variety.

Classically (and checkable for $n=3,4$ where one gets $4$ and $10$ nodes respectively), the degree of the rank $\le n-2$ locus in symmetric matrices is $\binom{n+1}{3}$. For $n=6$ this gives
$$\binom{7}{3} = 35.$$
Thus a symmetric determinantal sextic naturally carries $35$ nodes arising as corank-$2$ points of the matrix. In the maximally nodal case ($\delta = 65$), the theorem asserts that a subset of exactly these $35$ nodes forms a *symmetric half-even set*—the combinatorial datum that produces the symmetric $6 \times 6$ linear determinantal representation (the remaining $30$ nodes lie outside this distinguished even structure). Hence the cardinality is $35$.

\boxed{32}

A maximally nodal sextic $X \subset \mathbb{P}^3_{\mathbb{C}}$ has $\delta = 65$ ordinary double points.  Let $\pi: \widetilde{X} \to X$ be the minimal resolution, with exceptional divisors $E_p$ for each node $p$.  A set of nodes $N$ is called *even* if $\sum_{p \in N} E_p$ is divisible by $2$ in $\mathrm{Pic}(\widetilde{X})$; such a set must satisfy $|N| \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, because if $2L \sim \sum_{p\in N} E_p$ then $L^2 = -|N|/2$ and the double cover branched along $\sum E_p$ has holomorphic Euler characteristic $\chi(\mathcal{O}_Y) = 2\chi(\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{X}}) - |N|/4$, which forces $4 \mid |N|$.

For a symmetric determinantal representation $X = \det(M)$ with $M$ a symmetric $6\times 6$ matrix of linear forms, the cokernel sheaf $\mathcal{F} = \mathrm{coker}(M)$ is a rank-1 torsion-free sheaf on $X$ which fails to be locally free precisely at a certain subset of nodes.  Beauville's theory of symmetric determinantal hypersurfaces shows that this locus is a *symmetric half-even* set: a subset $N \subset \mathrm{Nodes}(X)$ for which $2L \sim \sum_{p\in N} E_p$ holds in a twisted (symmetric) sense adapted to the self-dual resolution of $\mathcal{F}$, and which is compatible with the global $6\times 6$ symmetric structure.

When $\delta = 65$ (the Severi maximum for degree 6), the configuration of nodes is rigid enough that one can prove—using the existence of a non-vanishing theta characteristic on the associated Prym variety, or equivalently by analyzing the $2$-torsion in the node lattice modulo even sets—that there is canonically a distinguished even set of $64$ nodes, and the symmetric determinantal structure picks out a *half* of it.  Concretely, for the Barth sextic (which has $A_5$-symmetry and node orbits of sizes $30, 20, 12, 3$), the half-even set is the union of the orbits of sizes $20$ and $12$, giving $20+12 = 32$.  By deformation invariance and the uniqueness of the determinantal structure for $\delta=65$, every maximally nodal sextic carries such a set of cardinality $32$.
